items.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
items.content: <article>The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, the insurance trade body, the ABI said.</article>
items.lbText:
A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters.

The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said.

Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said.

There was £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year.

At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts.

"As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them."

Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers."

He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg".

One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets , external .

The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said.

In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search.

Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed.

Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims.

In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims.

Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified.

This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said.

Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out there

Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix

H ow often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week , or 156 meals a year.

Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious.

We hear a lot about grocery stores and restaurants throwing out perfectly edible food, but they are just a small part of the problem. The vast majority of food waste , about 850m meals, comes from farms, followed by food manufacturing facilities with 178m meals, another 71m from the hospitality and food service sector, and finally 12m meals from the retail sector.

When I say easily accessible, I mean this is food we have the capacity to rescue and get to people. The organisation I head, Felix, is a food rescue charity. We recover edible surplus food that would otherwise go to waste and get it to more than 8,000 organisations that do amazing work to feed people in need. This food sustains lunch clubs for older people where friendships are forged and isolation is addressed. It supports food pantries, where families can access a weekly bag of shopping for just a few pounds. And it can provide meals in homelessness shelters and refuges. But with food insecurity rising, so too is the need for the food we recover. So we must rescue more of that billion-meal surplus.

In our food system, unavoidable surplus food is generated at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, unpredictable weather, grading standards and mismatches between harvest volumes and buyer orders contribute to the enormous quantities of edible produce without a home. But we are working with farmers to ensure this food is getting to people’s plates; almost half the food we gave out last year was fresh fruit and vegetables.

In manufacturing, production overruns, packaging changes and quality control measures create surplus that cannot be sold through normal channels. But there are bright spots – and an incredible example is the food manufacturer Premier Foods. When their noodle nests don’t pass quality control, we take them and use a partner organisation to repack and label them. We are doing a similar project with 2 Sisters Food Group, a huge manufacturing company that uses late-night surplus factory capacity to repack breaded chicken with minor visual defects.

We are also working with supermarkets such as Asda, Co-op, Ocado, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose. They give us a huge amount of stock that we get straight back out to every part of the UK.

So many companies are doing their bit, but the reason many are not is economics. It is cheaper for a business to waste food than to give it to people: the corporation tax system does not reward food donation in the same way it does a financial one. In addition, public subsidies for alternative disposal routes – such as turning food waste into animal food or biogas – provide profit. This creates a market that actively pulls surplus away from human consumption. We must change this.

That is why Felix has started the Redistribution Revolution. Felix, City Harvest, Community Shop, The Bread and Butter Thing, His Church, Feeding Britain, Neighbourly and the wider Felix and Xcess Networks have formed the Food Redistribution Partnership UK, working together to rescue more food. Backed by the government, we have launched a national programme to redistribute surplus food that aims to triple the amount of food we redistribute over the next decade. According to our research, about 1% of all excess food in the UK food system is redistributed by charities. France redistributes about twice that , while the US does three times more.

Our revolution needs food businesses to make redistribution the default route for all surplus food, and view it as an opportunity for social good. We need philanthropists to invest in the infrastructure required to store and move the food. And we need the government to change the tax system and make it more financially viable for companies to get food to people.

Finally, we need donations and volunteers to help us rescue and deliver more food.

We know surplus food is out there, and while it is very important to recognise that redistribution is not a systemic solution to poverty, we are certain that good food is going to waste. Rescuing it can be a powerful way to alleviate the symptoms of food insecurity, and to support organisations that are helping people tackle the challenges in their lives.

Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix

items.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
items.content: <article>Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.</article>
items.lbText:
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.

"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.

Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.

When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.

"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.

"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."

Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.

"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.

The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.

Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.

This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.

The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".

"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.

"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.

The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.

"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

items.title: Irish budget tackles childcare and energy costs
items.content: <article>The threshold at which people start paying the higher income tax rate is also expected to increase.</article>
items.lbText:
The Irish government is expected to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs when it delivers its budget later.

The threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax is also expected to be increased from its current level of €44,000 (£37,000).

The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said the budget has to be about "trying to ease the pressure on families and households".

The broad shape of the budget was set out in the Summer Economic Statement , external , promising tax measures worth €1.5bn (£1.27bn) and extra spending of €7bn (£5.92bn).

Much of that additional spending is "standstill" funding to cover the rising costs of current services.

Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services.

Figures released last week showed the country is expected to run a surplus of €6.9bn (£5.84bn) this year, lower than the €9.2bn (£7.79bn) forecast in April.

That smaller forecast surplus reflects the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overspends, particularly in health.

Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments.

A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised the government for not saving more.

Other measures expected to be announced on Tuesday are a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK ISA.

A proposal for a "culture card" for teenagers, to spend on events like concerts, is also set to be announced though the value and eligibility are unclear.

items.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
items.content: <article>In the internet age, medium-sized retail hubs are looking for new ways to survive and thrive.</article>
items.lbText:
The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide.

"It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973.

Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw.

Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling.

Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left.

That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year .

But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space.

"It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me."

In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema.

There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre.

This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country.

So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls?

"There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre.

"The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet."

Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE , external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres.

Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres.

"It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton.

Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds.

Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops.

"The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open."

The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses.

Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing.

But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down.

Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space .

"Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use.

This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton.

Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg.

"Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got."

What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities.

Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible.

Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store.

George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

"We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.'

"That is how we can get other people to join us."

items.title: Banks still refusing credit cards, watchdog says
items.content: <article>Applications are being denied despite a change to make it easier, Jersey Consumer Council says.</article>
items.lbText:
Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said.

The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications .

However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks.

A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision".

Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared.

"The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said.

"We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not."

A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies".

"This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said.

"It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey.

"The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so."

items.lbText:
Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more

A s fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas.

In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise.

While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate.

Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children.

“You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says.

In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay.

“It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says.

About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, mainly on the largest islands of Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders.

“The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says.

Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry.

“You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says.

Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work.

“Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.”

Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back.

“A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says.

Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage. With almost no public transport, he says he needs to drive to work because of how rural it is. The cost of his commute has meant sacrificing some of the things he likes to do with his girlfriend.

“Me and my girlfriend like to go to restaurants that are a bit of a distance away, around half an hour drive. We’ve not done that in a while. I think it’s safe to say that the cost of fuel will be affecting businesses because they’ll be getting fewer customers,” he says.

As fuel costs rise, islanders have started taking jerry cans to the mainland to stock up on cheaper fuel, even to just save a few pennies a litre, Ryan says. Normally, the cans are used in the winter to stock up when high winds and choppy seas disrupt deliveries to the islands and pumps run dry.…

items.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
items.author: Gaby Hinsliff
items.content:
Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it

There’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.

And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

items.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
items.author: Morwenna Ferrier
items.content:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?

Temperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”

I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.

items.title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
items.content: <article>The world's fastest growing major economy has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. </article>
items.lbText:
India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.

But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.

The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.

Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.

On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.

It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.

Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.

This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.

Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.

Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return.

"This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins."

India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.

While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.

With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs.

These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise.

For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency.

The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets.

Stock valuations have been another major concern.

The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors.

"Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years.

However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits.

In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story.

"Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition."

India seeks AI breakthrough - but is it falling behind?

And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds.

While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie.

Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein.

"We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade."

There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward.

"Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage, though trade tensions and higher energy prices remain a “challenge for corporate performance going ahead”.

For now, while foreign investors may have given up, Indian savers, even though increasingly more anxious, haven't slowed their monthly investment flows , external into mutual funds.…

items.title: Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget
items.content: <article>Shadow ministers unveiled a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.</article>
items.lbText:
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights.

Speaking at the party's conference in Birmingham, Griffith said "lower, simpler and fairer taxes" would be his "personal north star" although he noted his ambition for cuts would take place "only when we can afford to do so".

He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government between 2010 and 2024.

Speaking on the main stage, Griffith said: "No country in history has ever taxed its way to prosperity, so we will cut taxes, but only when we can afford to do so, and always saying clearly how we will fund that within our golden economic rule."

The party's "golden economic rule" involves at least half of all savings identified going towards "deficit reduction, with the other half going to tax cuts and pro-growth measures".

Griffith likened his approach to that of former Tory Chancellor Nigel Lawson, adding: "It's my ambition to scrap at least one tax every budget. What would we prioritise? There's a lot.

"Tax cuts that help growth, tax cuts that improve incentives to work, tax cuts that make life simpler and fairer."

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would be scrapped by the Conservatives.

Griffith sought to signal a different approach under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, telling members that the EPR was the "sort of thing the old Conservative Party went along with".

He also said Labour plans a "vindicative raid on family homes" in the form of the HVCTS, also dubbed the "mansion tax", which he would seek to scrap.

The shadow chancellor said: "It's an anti-growth tax that will distort the housing market and remove the incentive to make home improvements."

Ahead of his speech, Griffith was pressed on BBC Breakfast on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing.

Griffith said: "We are going to keep it."

In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others".

Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable.

Properties worth more than £2m in England face mansion tax

Tories committed to pension triple lock, deputy leader says

Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow

During a series of speeches on Monday, Griffith and other shadow ministers also announced further details on the policies they believe will help free up businesses and grow the economy.

The proposals included ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, such as the future homes standard.

Griffith said the next Conservative government would support a third runway at Heathrow Airport. Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

The Conservatives also want to implement a single levy for developers in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

Prospect general secretary Mike Clancy, whose union represents members in Natural England and the Environment Agency, said: "Conservative budget cuts have left these regulators struggling to perform their vital functions with 'lack of resources' the most common reason for planning delays.

"The solution is to restore their funding to adequate levels, not scrap vital safeguards."

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth, anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn."

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 .

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said scrapping rules that "secure affordable homes and vital community infrastructure is not a plan for growth".

She added: "It is a gift to developers, leaving communities to pick up the bill for new housing while handing ordinary people higher costs and fewer protections."

items.title: BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible | Nils Pratley
items.author: Nils Pratley
items.content:
For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes

“All the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk. Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.

Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.

For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes

BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobs

“A ll the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk . Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.

Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.

OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately.

Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvement on the last one . As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control.

The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well.

That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution.

The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement with BT , however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money.

The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty.

It’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.

items.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
items.content: <article>It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools.</article>
items.lbText:
The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.

The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement.

Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August.

But multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.

It is not clear why the defence department has stopped using the company's tools now. The details of the department cutting ties entirely have not been previously reported.

Anthropic had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.

But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI tools.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.

Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules

Anthropic sues US government for calling it a risk

Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down

As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.

OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department

The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.

It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.

Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.

"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.

"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.

Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.

Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.

The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.

Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.

Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration.

Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week.

After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI.

"How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".

Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

items.lbText:
Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise

The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.

Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.

In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise .

Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages .

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.

She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”

The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.

Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.

There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September .

Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability. He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

items.title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk
items.content: <article>The takeover still needs to be approved by the regulator, but would give certainty to TalkTalk's millions of customers</article>
items.lbText:
The UK's biggest broadband provider, BT, has agreed to rescue rival operator TalkTalk in a takeover .

The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal.

Some have raised concerns about the increased control BT will have over the broadband market as a result of the deal.

BT chief executive Alison Kirkby said the deal provided "a safety net" for those who customers rely on TalkTalk. The administrator said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff.

TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK.

BT said the deal would provide "much needed and immediate reassurance" for TalkTalk's employees as well as its UK customers.

"This includes vulnerable households, and connections that support critical national infrastructure providers across health, emergency services, defence, education, transport, banking and government."

TalkTalk began as a challenger to BT in the broadband market. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange, but was taken over by private equity in 2021.

Since then, the firm has built up debt while losing customers, leaving it unable to pay some of those it owes money to.

The Competition Markets Authority (CMA) will need to approve the takeover, which would give BT greater power over the broadband market.

Tom Smith, a competition lawyer and former legal director at the CMA, said the regulator will be balancing that concern with other considerations.

"When the CMA looks at it, it will look at what would have happened if the deal wasn't going through," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"If TalkTalk would have exited the market, for example, then really any deal is better than TalkTalk exiting, but then there might be alternative bidders as well that would have been less anticompetitive."

BT has said it will cost the firm £400m to buy TalkTalk.

This includes the amount needed to buy TalkTalk from administration, fees, TalkTalk's £60m loss for this year, and BT effectively writing off the £100m TalkTalk owes BT's Openreach business.

items.title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
items.content: <article>At least 23 huge data centres are planned in Scotland, causing significant concern for campaigners.</article>
items.lbText:
Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes.

Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale.

The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world.

Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres.

Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs.

Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make.

So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles?

From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse.

On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI.

While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering.

Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense.

One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife .

The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches.

AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves.

At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie , which has a capacity for 12MW.

The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level.

If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.

At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village.

noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems

The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.

The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium.

One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector.

Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed.

However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy .

During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking.

As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating.

While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain.

An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead.

Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife.

As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs.

Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart.

When it was announced in January , external , £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised.

The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated.

About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships. The rest are in construction.

Apatura - the developer behind 10 of the hyperscale data centre proposals in Scotland - highlights its green credentials with its access to renewable energy and battery storage.

With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind.

The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone.

In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity.

A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force.

However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted.

The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season.

items.title: Trump chooses top spy boss to run new AI taskforce
items.content: <article>The US president said his national intelligence chief will lead the group as worries over AI grow.</article>
items.lbText:
US President Donald Trump has unveiled a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.

It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".

Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" regulation pact.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.

Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.

It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.

On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.

The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.

"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.

Over the weekend, a former leader in OpenAI's Safety Systems team wrote in an article for the Atlantic magazine that he had left the firm because its culture was "broken".

"As [OpenAI] sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," wrote David Robinson, who was involved in safety and transparency reporting.

The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Last month, the ChatGPT-maker pulled the release of its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

Its AI models have come under scrutiny after a series of cyber security incidents involving its technology, including an unauthorised breach of Australian government systems .

Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit

OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns

Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.

The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding , arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.

Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.

"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.

The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.

Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump .

items.title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
items.content: <article>The cost of a new fixed-rate mortgage has been rising in recent weeks as lenders face higher costs.</article>
items.lbText:
The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show.

The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs.

It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals.

Moneyfacts said that the biggest High Street lenders had made repeated fixed rate increases during September. Barclays increased selected fixed rates on four occasions, while HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander and TSB each made three rounds of increases.

It meant that the average rate on a new five-year deal was at its highest since September 2023. On two-year deals, the average rate is at its highest since December 2023.

It should be used as a guide only and does not represent the suitability, eligibility or availability of mortgage offers for users. For exact figures, users will need to approach an official mortgage lender.

Interest rates fluctuate based on the Bank of England's base rate and market conditions

"Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts.

"Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed."

She said that those coming to the end of a fixed deal would be "wise to seek advice and compare deals carefully".

Some lenders could allow people to lock in a rate three months before their current deal ends, while others could allow six months, she said.

Springall said rate rises were "inevitable" because lenders' wholesale funding costs had climbed as a result of rising gilt yields .

Interest rates - known as the yield - on government bonds have been going up, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.

The knock-on impact of this on the mortgage market has meant that the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% has plunged by 99%, from 1,494 since the start of September 2026 to nine now.

In contrast, the number of sub-5% variable rate mortgages has remained broadly stable, Springall said, leading some borrowers to chose deals that track the Bank of England's base rate.

Millions of mortgage-holders are coming to the end of their current deals in the next two years.

Just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028, according to Bank of England forecasts.

Some may have expected rates to have fallen this year, owing to improved economic conditions, but the Iran war has upended many of those expectations.

It has also led to wider pressure on the cost of essential bills.

On Friday, drivers saw the average cost of diesel rise above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group.

Domestic energy prices also rose by 4% at the start of October, and forecasters have predicted a 16% increase when regulator Ofgem sets its next price cap for January.

The government is under pressure to support those most likely to struggle to pay at the Budget later this month.

items.lbText:
Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death

W e booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking.

In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact.

Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered.

Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required.

We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence.

My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue.

Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now.

I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information.

When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death.

The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing.

The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”.

Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died.

Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none.

Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you.

A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.”

Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be.

“We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC . “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.”

MS , meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.”

We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions .
